title: Lowest Common Ancestor with Binary Lifting
directAnswer: To answer many LCA queries on a fixed rooted tree, precompute `up[node][j]` = the 2^j-th ancestor of node, for j up to log n. Build it with one DFS for depths plus the recurrence `up[v][j] = up[ up[v][j-1] ][j-1]`. To answer LCA(a, b): lift the deeper node up to the other's depth, then lift both in powers of two while their ancestors differ. Preprocessing is O(n log n); each query is O(log n).

remember.pattern: Sparse ancestor table — jump in powers of two using up[v][j] = up[up[v][j-1]][j-1]
remember.formula:
up[v][0] = parent[v]
up[v][j] = up[ up[v][j-1] ][j-1]
lca(a, b):
  level a, b to equal depth, then
  for j in high..0: if up[a][j] != up[b][j]: a, b = up[a][j], up[b][j]
  return up[a][0]
rules: `up[v][0]` is the direct parent; the root's parent is a **sentinel** (itself or 0/-1) so lifts past the root stay safe.
Allocate `LOG = ceil(log2(n)) + 1` levels — enough to cover the deepest possible jump.
**Equalize depths first**: lift the deeper node by the depth difference, decomposed into powers of two.
Then lift **both** nodes by the largest jump that keeps their ancestors *different*; the answer is the parent of where they stop.
If after equalizing the nodes are already equal, that node **is** the LCA — handle it before the binary search.
whenToUse: Many LCA queries on a static rooted tree (the tree does not change between queries)
k-th ancestor queries, or distance(u, v) = depth[u] + depth[v] − 2·depth[lca]
Jump-pointer problems: 'follow parent 2^j times' on any functional graph
Path queries on trees that reduce to ancestor lookups
antiSignals: Tree changes between queries (links added/removed) → use link-cut trees or Euler-tour + segment tree
Only one or two LCA queries → a single O(n) walk-up is simpler than O(n log n) preprocessing
It is actually a BST → LCA is a single O(h) descent comparing values, no lifting needed
You need LCA on a DAG, not a tree → binary lifting assumes a unique parent per node
remember.takeaway: Binary lifting turns 'walk up k steps' from O(k) into O(log k) by precomputing power-of-two jumps — the same doubling trick behind fast exponentiation and sparse tables. LCA falls out by aligning depths and then binary-searching the highest point where the two paths still diverge.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can design O(n log n) preprocessing that makes each query O(log n), and whether you correctly handle the two-phase query: equalize depths, then lift both nodes while ancestors differ.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Returning the node where the lifts meet instead of its parent, forgetting the already-an-ancestor case (one node is the LCA), or sizing the up table with too few levels so a deep jump runs off the end.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Derive LOG from n, explain the doubling recurrence in one line, and note that distance and k-th ancestor reuse the same table. Mention the iterative DFS to avoid stack overflow on a tree that is a long chain.

problemStatement:
You are given a rooted tree with `n` nodes (the parent of each node, with the root having no parent). Answer up to `q` queries, each asking for the ***lowest common ancestor*** of two nodes `a` and `b` — the deepest node that is an ancestor of both.

Preprocess once, then answer every query in ***O(log n)***.
constraints: The tree is rooted and static (does not change between queries)
Nodes are 0-indexed (or 1-indexed); the root has a sentinel parent
understanding: We have one fixed rooted tree and a flood of LCA queries. A single naive walk-up per query is O(n) and too slow in aggregate. Binary lifting precomputes, for every node, its ancestor 1, 2, 4, 8, … steps above. With those jump pointers we can move any node up by an arbitrary amount in O(log n) by combining powers of two, and the LCA reduces to aligning depths and then jumping both nodes as high as possible while they stay on different branches.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the tree static across queries?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Binary lifting precomputes ancestor tables once; if the tree changed between queries we would need a dynamic structure like link-cut trees instead.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How many queries relative to n?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Many — that is what justifies O(n log n) preprocessing. For a single query, a plain O(n) walk-up is simpler and just as fast.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could the tree be a long chain (degenerate)?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, depth can reach n. The DFS that fills depths should be iterative (explicit stack) so a chain of 2×10⁵ nodes does not overflow the recursion stack.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do we also need distance or k-th ancestor?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: If so, the same up table answers them: k-th ancestor by decomposing k into set bits, and distance(u,v) = depth[u] + depth[v] − 2·depth[lca(u,v)].

examples.explanation: 3 and 4 are both children of 1, so their lowest common ancestor is 1.
3 is under 1, 5 is under 2; the only shared ancestor is the root 0.
1 is itself an ancestor of 4, so the LCA is 1 — the 'one node is an ancestor of the other' case.

approaches.name: Baseline — Walk Both Pointers Up to the Root
approaches.whenToMention: Say this first: it is the obvious correct method and it sets the depth/alignment idea that the optimal reuses.

complexity.time: O(n) per query after O(n) depth setup

hints: First make both nodes the same depth: lift the deeper one parent-by-parent until depths match.
Then move both up one step at a time in lockstep; the first node where they coincide is the LCA.
Each query can walk the whole height of the tree — O(n) per query. With many queries that is too slow, which motivates jump pointers.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Equalizing depths is up to O(n) parent steps, and the lockstep walk is up to O(n) more. With q queries this is O(q·n) in the worst case (e.g. a chain).
approaches.explanation:
The direct method needs only parent pointers and a depth for each node.

**Step one — equalize depth.** An LCA cannot be deeper than the shallower of the two nodes. So first lift the deeper node up, one parent at a time, until both nodes sit at the same depth.

**Step two — climb in lockstep.** Now move both nodes up one parent at a time together. As long as they differ, keep going; the moment they point at the same node, that node is the LCA. They are guaranteed to meet no later than the root.

**Why it is correct.** Once depths are equal, the two upward paths to the root have the same length and converge exactly at the LCA — every node above the LCA is shared, every node below is on a separate branch.

**Why it is too slow.** Each phase can traverse the entire height of the tree, which is O(n) for a chain. Answering q queries this way is O(q·n) — fine for a handful of queries, hopeless for 2×10⁵ of them. The fix is to take *big* upward jumps (powers of two) instead of single steps, which is exactly binary lifting.
approaches.insight: The two-phase structure — equalize depth, then climb together — is identical in the optimal solution. Binary lifting changes only *how* you climb: instead of one step at a time, you take the largest power-of-two jump that does not overshoot, cutting O(n) climbing to O(log n).

java.line: stack.push(new int[]{root, root, 0});  // node, par, dep
java.explanation: Iterative DFS so a chain of 2×10⁵ nodes does not overflow the recursion stack.
Equalize depth by lifting the deeper node one parent at a time.

java.line: while (a != b) { a = parent[a]; b = parent[b]; }
java.explanation: Lockstep climb; the meeting point is the LCA. This loop is the O(n) bottleneck.

python.line: stack = [(root, root, 0)]      # iterative DFS, no recursion limit risk
python.explanation: Explicit stack instead of recursion — safe on long chains.
Bring both nodes to the same depth first.
Single-step lockstep climb — correct but O(n) per query.

pitfalls: Recursive DFS on a chain of 2×10⁵ nodes — stack overflow; use an explicit stack.
Climbing before equalizing depths — the pointers can pass each other and never meet.
Accepting O(n) per query — fine for one query, far too slow for many.

approaches.name: Binary Lifting — Sparse Ancestor Table (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want for many queries. 'Precompute the 2^j-th ancestor of every node, then jump in powers of two.'

complexity.time: O(n log n) preprocess, O(log n) per query

hints: Store up[v][j] = the ancestor of v that is 2^j steps above it. up[v][0] is just the parent.
Fill the table by doubling: a 2^j jump is two 2^(j-1) jumps, so up[v][j] = up[ up[v][j-1] ][j-1]. Compute level by level.

Query in two phases: lift the deeper node by the depth gap (decomposed into powers of two), then for j from high to low, jump BOTH nodes up by 2^j whenever their ancestors there differ. The LCA is the parent of where they stop.
approaches.complexityReasoning: The table has n rows and log n columns, each filled in O(1) → O(n log n) build. A query does at most log n jumps to equalize depth plus log n jumps in the second phase → O(log n) per query. Space is the table, O(n log n).
approaches.explanation:
Binary lifting precomputes jump pointers so any upward movement becomes a handful of power-of-two hops.

**The table.** Define `up[v][j]` as the ancestor reached by climbing `2^j` parents from `v`. The base level is the parent: `up[v][0] = parent[v]`. The doubling recurrence builds the rest: climbing `2^j` steps is the same as climbing `2^(j-1)` steps and then `2^(j-1)` steps again, so `up[v][j] = up[ up[v][j-1] ][j-1]`. Because each higher level depends only on the level below, fill the table column by column (all `j-1` before any `j`). With `LOG = ⌈log₂ n⌉ + 1` columns, the deepest possible jump is covered.

**Jumping by an arbitrary amount.** To climb exactly `k` steps, write `k` in binary and take one jump per set bit: for each bit `j` set in `k`, replace `v` with `up[v][j]`. Since `k < n` has at most `log₂ n` set bits, this is `O(log n)`.

**Query phase 1 — equalize depth.** Suppose `depth[a] ≥ depth[b]`. Lift `a` up by `depth[a] − depth[b]` using the bit decomposition above, so both nodes sit at the same depth. If `a == b` now, one node was an ancestor of the other and *that node is the LCA* — return it immediately. Missing this check is a classic bug.

**Query phase 2 — rise to just below the LCA.** Now both nodes are at equal depth but on (possibly) different branches. For `j` from the highest level down to 0, look at `up[a][j]` and `up[b][j]`: if they are *different*, jump both up by `2^j` (their ancestors still differ, so the LCA is higher). If they are the *same*, that jump would overshoot — skip it. After the loop, `a` and `b` sit on different branches but their parents coincide: the LCA is `up[a][0]`.

**Why scanning j from high to low works.** It is a binary search on the climb distance. Greedily taking the biggest jump that keeps the two nodes distinct lands them exactly one step below the LCA — every set bit of the true distance gets taken once, none overshoots. The sentinel parent at the root makes 'jump past the root' return the root, so out-of-range jumps are harmless.
approaches.insight: Binary lifting is the doubling trick applied to the parent function: precompute `f^(2^j)` so you can apply `f` any number of times in O(log n). The LCA query is then a depth alignment followed by a binary search for the highest divergence point. The exact same table answers k-th-ancestor and, via depths, path distance — one preprocessing, many queries.

dryRun.intro: up[v][0] = parent. LOG = 3. Phase 1 (depths already equal) then phase 2 jumps both while ancestors differ.

java.explanation: Number of columns = ⌈log2 n⌉ + 1 (at least 1), enough for the deepest jump.
Base level is the direct parent; the root's parent is itself (sentinel).
Doubling: a 2^j jump is two 2^(j-1) jumps chained.
Lift the deeper node by the depth gap, one set bit at a time.
After equalizing, equal nodes mean one was an ancestor of the other — that IS the LCA.

java.line: if (up[a][j] != up[b][j]) { a = up[a][j]; b = up[b][j]; }
java.explanation: Jump both up only while their ancestors differ; stop just below the LCA.
The nodes are one step below the LCA, so its parent is the answer.

python.explanation: bit_length() of n gives ⌈log2(n+1)⌉ — enough columns for any jump.
Parent pointer is the 2^0 ancestor; root points to itself.
Compose two half-size jumps to get the 2^j jump.
Decompose the depth difference into powers of two and lift accordingly.
Ancestor case — return immediately before the second phase.
Greedy biggest non-overshooting jump — binary search for the divergence point.
Parent of the stopping node is the lowest common ancestor.

edgeCases.behavior: Depths equal, a == b after phase 1 → returns the node itself.

edgeCases.input: One node is an ancestor of the other
edgeCases.behavior: After equalizing depth the deeper node lifts onto the shallower one; the a == b check returns it as the LCA.
The root's sentinel parent (itself) makes over-long jumps stay at the root, so up[][j] never indexes out of range.

pitfalls: Returning the meeting node from phase 2 instead of its parent (up[a][0]).
Skipping the a == b check after depth alignment — wrong on the ancestor case.
Too few columns (LOG) so a deep jump runs off the table.
Recursive DFS for the depth/parent setup — stack overflow on a chain; use an explicit stack.

commonMistakes: Returning the node where the two lifts stop instead of its parent.
Forgetting the case where one node is already an ancestor of the other.
Allocating too few levels in the up table, so a deep jump overruns it.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Returning the stop node, not its parent
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Phase 2 deliberately stops one level BELOW the LCA (where the two nodes are still on different branches). The answer is their common parent, up[a][0] — returning a itself gives a wrong, too-deep node.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the ancestor case
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If b is an ancestor of a, then after lifting a to b's depth we get a == b. Without an early return, phase 2's loop never moves (ancestors are already equal at every level) and you return up[a][0] = the parent of b, which is wrong.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Too few ancestor levels
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If LOG is smaller than ⌈log2 n⌉ + 1, the largest jump cannot reach the root from the deepest node, so depth alignment and the rise loop both miss high ancestors.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: self.LOG = 16        # hard-coded; breaks when n needs more bits
commonMistakesDetailed.good: self.LOG = max(1, n.bit_length())   # scales with n

followupVariations.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
followupVariations.hint: For a single query on a general binary tree, a one-pass recursion is simpler than building lifting tables.

followupVariations.title: Kth Ancestor of a Tree Node
followupVariations.hint: Exactly the up[][] table — decompose k into set bits and take one jump per bit.

followupVariations.title: Distance Between Two Nodes
followupVariations.hint: depth[u] + depth[v] − 2·depth[lca(u, v)] reuses the same preprocessing.

followupVariations.title: Euler Tour of a Tree
followupVariations.hint: An alternative LCA route: Euler tour + range-minimum on depths answers LCA in O(1) after O(n log n) build.

patternNote: Binary lifting: precompute up[v][j] = the 2^j-th ancestor via the doubling recurrence up[v][j] = up[up[v][j-1]][j-1]. Answer LCA by equalizing depth then binary-searching the highest divergence point — O(n log n) build, O(log n) query. The same table powers k-th ancestor and path-distance queries on static rooted trees.
